A single-player campaign of Counter-Strike is an alien concept to many, but it does exist! In the Hard setting, this is extremely difficult, which is good for CS veterans. Even though I'm personally acquainted with how Goldsrc AI works, this was still a tough game to play through. This feels somewhat like a mix of Call of Duty with Tom Clancy games. The plot changes completely every mission, so there's no full story at all. Deleted Scenes plays out like a Half-Life game, with maps loading one after the other.

It's impressive how sometimes we seem to find physics at play, like enemies being propelled backwards after getting shot, corpses falling down the stairs, snipers falling from heights in "ragdoll" looking states, a paper map is thrown and looks realistic in Mission 4, and an enemy falling and getting impaled. Physics are nothing too impressive nowadays, but once we realize that in this game they're actually pre-rendered moments choreographed by set animations rather than actual engine stunts, it's amazing to watch them at play!

If you're a Half-Life fan, this is the game for you. Despite questionable voice acting, Counter-Strike: Condition Zero Deleted Scenes is way beyond decent, and is actually cut content from what Condition Zero ended up being. Don't play the final product, it's a waste of time, play Deleted Scenes instead!

🔫 ☣️ Counter-Strike: Condition Zero (Deleted Scenes) – let's be 100% real, this game is total, unadulterated garbage. Huge props to you for actually finishing every single level, because enduring that entire grind is a serious test of patience for a game that just shouldn't exist.You hit the nail right on the head: they desperately wanted to build a narrative, scripted single-player experience like Half-Life, but trying to force that layout onto the Counter-Strike engine completely flopped.

The core gameplay loop is incredibly shallow and dated. There is zero tactical depth, zero economy management, and absolutely no teamwork. All you do is mindlessly run down narrow, linear corridors and shoot waves of repetitive enemies. Occasionally, the game forces you to "think" by throwing in a basic puzzle like using a blowtorch or defusing a bomb, but it's just cheap padding to hide how boring the shooting actually is.

What makes it worse is the notorious development history behind it. The game was tossed around like a hot potato between four different development studios, and it shows. The enemy AI is completely broken—they alternate between being totally brain-dead and instantly wall-hacking you through solid objects with perfect aimbot precision. It completely strips away everything that makes Counter-Strike great and leaves you with a clunky, frustrating relic of the early 2000s.

🟢 A weirdly interesting piece of gaming history if you want to see old, unused GoldSrc engine assets
🔴 Awkward, linear level design that completely fails to capture the cinematic genius of Half-Life
🌀 An incredibly tedious and repetitive loop of running, killing mindless bots, and hitting basic triggers
🤖 Frustrating enemy AI that switches from completely blind to unfair aimbot headshots in a split second

The Deleted Scenes singleplayer mode is a curiosity for fans of Goldsrc games in general, but I cannot recommend it on its actual merits as an FPS. The gunplay is good, as should be expected of a game based off of Counter-Strike, and the graphics and maps are very detailed for a Goldsrc game, but the actual gameplay has a lot of flaws and poor design choices that sour the experience.

There's basically one type of fight that happens for the entire game: A situation where all enemies in an area are sitting in various corners lying in wait for you, sometimes opening a door to bait you into the next ambush. Even when allies are around, fighting nearby, or supposedly passing through an area, enemies will spontaneously generate in ambush points even if it meant they ran past allies, or allies ran past them, or they somehow hid somewhere while you killed dozens of their allies. Oftentimes this game will put you in view of snipers before you could possibly see them. Certain enemies will have drastically more health despite being visibly less armored than the fifty henchmen you gunned down to get to them. Some levels overload you with weapons despite whatever AR you started with fulfilling every role you could possibly need. Enemy variety is extremely sparse, and when combined with every encounter being the same exact ambush, the levels end up feeling samey even if the game constantly varies its locations. The stealth "mechanics" which might have varied up the combat are just glorified scripted sequences where you cannot fight and game over if spotted.

Ultimately there's a lot of annoyances that pile up even if the game looks good and has some fun set pieces. Considering how this game came out a couple months before Half-Life 2, but doesn't even manage to take lessons from [i]Half-Life 1[/i], I'd have been insulted if I paid full price for this back in the day. Luckily nowadays it can be picked up on sale for cheap.

I'd only recommend if you are a Goldsrc head and have ran out of random Half-Life campaign mods to play.

You are given an world map and take the role of different spec ops teams from around the globe (even Russia which is interesting to see them portrayed as good guys from a western developer). You never play as the terrorists which sucks since its half of CS' identity. 

Since you aren't here for the story, is the gameplay and level design any good at least? Ehhhhh... while the game is built on source, an engine dear to my heart and one renowned for its interesting physics. It has been completely gutted here, patching out fun mechanics like bhopping making the boring level design even more prominent. Did I mention the levels completely blow? Ok that's not all true, some are really interesting! Pretty much every level designed by Russell Meakim has an interesting setting combined with a good selection of weapons. However even these fall victim to some noticeable design flaws. I played all levels at max difficulty, which revealed how poorly placed enemies can be. Sometimes they mimic real CS being tucked in tight corners that you have to clear on entries. This is fine however often they can be placed at the start and ends of ladders and climbing objects. If you've ever played CS you'd know this is fucked up. So whenever I got on a ladder I would get one-tapped (due to high difficulty) with no way to defend myself. My skills aren't being tested here, just my patience.

Anyways some are worth playing some are pretty bad filler, if you're super curious I'd say give it a go. If anything atleast you get the wildest credit scene to send you out.

I never noticed that CounterStrike had a single player edition until 2023. 
I had fun with it, figuring out the endless series of surprise situations the game put you in. 
Some notes on the game are:
- Enemy AI is weak, they basically attack when a trap is sprung or stand still.
- Enemies need multiple shots to the head before going down. 
So its not really possible to progress without getting shot yourself, 
but you can take a good number of hits too before you die.
- You start missions with low ammo and cannot pick up weapons or ammo from dead enemies (!!)
So in the start of every mission you have to be careful to find all ammo that lies around.
Luckily there is a cheat built in to give yourself more (realistic) ammo.
- Because of all the position-triggered traps, you'll have to save game a lot the first time through,
but the game fortunately does not limit that.
So I had quote a but of fun going through the missions in different "words" in 13 hours.
Cheers!

But the enemies become very overwhelming in the later levels, are often hard to locate, and can deal tons of damage, even on easy mode.

I did encounter two frustrating bugs in the game. it often crashes during random segments of gameplay, and half the times you load a save, it forces your weapon to fire automatically, which will alert enemies. You can stop it by clicking mouse1 and loading the save again, but its still very annoying.

After my profound disappointment with Counter-Strike Condition Zero, I was hardly expecting much from this expansion pack. The base game (which pretended to boast a 'single player campaign') is really just a collection of offline bot matches that gradually became difficult and unfun to the point of tedium, and I, having better things to do, moved on. But my God, if I had ANY inclination to believe that Deleted Scenes was literally a full-fledged story-based campaign made in the style of Half-Life then I would have played this years ago. To think that this has sat dormant in my Steam library for nearly an entire decade after purchasing the Valve pack, and for it to be THIS cool, is nearly dizzying.

Now, I'm not trying to sell you some kind of greatly underappreciated gem from a long-gone era of gaming, because this game is far from perfect. As a matter of fact, it's pretty unfinalised and in desperate need of some serious polish. I've tried reading into the game's history and it's so messy that I still can't make clear sense of it. It seems that it started as a project headed by Gearbox Software (best known at the time for their Half-Life expansions and its PlayStation 2 port) but when the studio parted ways with the Counter-Strike franchise it then went to a team called Ritual Entertainment, but - I think - their work was so derivative quality-wise from what Valve had expected that the reigns to the game were then handed to Turtle Rock Studios, who finished it themselves. That's how I think the story goes anyway. As I had mentioned earlier though, Turtle Rock completely botched the main game, and I wasn't exactly thrilled to try this one out. Amazingly, this expansion (Ritual apparently resented its 'Deleted Scenes' title) plays out almost exactly like some kind of undiscovered Half-Life game, set in the perspective of several counter-terrorism operatives. There's even a training sequence that you can tell is obviously inspired by Half-Life's hazard course, which triggered my fascination right from the get-go. 

The game is sadly something of an unfinished wreck at times though. I don't know who screwed it up, but 6 of the 18 total missions aren't actually sequenced into the campaign at all for some reason, despite its unconnected 'anthology' structure, and are simply included as 'extras' found on the world map screen. This wouldn't really be a huge deal, but it was a little jarring to play the Japanese subway mission (which actually happened to be the last one I did) only to be met by a freaking TITLE CARD for the game, indicating this was originally intended to be the first level of the campaign. 

Things get far worse than this though. Deleted Scenes WILL make you mad at some point or another. There are frankly way, way too many enemies in your path, and you're often fighting them all by yourself like you're Gordon Freeman or something. The terrorists unload AK-47s into your face from their convenient hiding spots the very moment you come around the corner, and their hitboxes can be appalling sometimes. Some of the missions involve stealth, which doesn't feel all that refined or even fun for that matter. And don't even get me started on the voice actors hamming it up with goofy lines and phony accents. Cringy doesn't begin to describe them. But no kidding, I couldn't even imagine playing this on hard mode, because I genuinely don't think there'd be enough health and bullets. I tell you, the game really pushes its luck sometimes. The scene where a terrorist triggers a timer for a nuclear bomb in the confines of an abandoned church is a great example of un-play-tested garbage. You have to kill him before you can start defusing, and this guy is some kind of otherworldly Superman villain who has about 100,000 hit points to his name. I think I had to reattempt this scene about twenty times before just barely pulling through. Talk about irritating. 

Yet, in spite of all its let downs, Deleted Scenes is still a thousand times more interesting than the main game, and it can honestly best be described as this bizarre lovechild that's the result of mixing GoldSource Half-Life and Counter-Strike together. If this game had been more of a success (or, ahem, had been given the attention it deserved from Valve) perhaps this series would have a lot more story-based modes to play in. 

I have to say that, with the possible exception of Call Of Duty 4 Modern Warfare, no video game has so perfectly captured that 2000s 'War On Terror' vibe like Deleted Scenes does.

Underrated gem. An actual first person shooter singleplayer campaign with real missions that controls and feels just like CS 1.6, without the team-based matches. I wish they made games like this more often. The best way I could describe this game is Ready Or Not, but it's not taking itself seriously in the slightest. It's fun, but there are some real problems. 

The buggy AI and janky gunplay can be chalked up to "it's old", but the biggest problem I encountered is how some missions are VERY FPS dependent. Movable objects become immovable and some NPC's pathing breaks at higher framerates so some missions (like the Japan one) become impossible to complete if you don't handicap your FPS. The weird thing is that even with fps_override 0, the game is supposed to have a max FPS of 100 (supposedly so that the physics engine doesn't break), but objects are still immovable at that FPS so you need to lower it to around 30.

One thing I absolutely LOVED about this game is how there's so many secret areas even for such a linear game. Some contain actual loot like armor and ammunition, but some contain easter eggs left by the developers.

This single-player Counter-Strike game is very weird to say the least.
It has a bunch of random counter terrorist mission scenarios that aren't really connected in any grand story (atleast I didn't pick up on any connected story). A couple of missions aren't even in the main "mission chain" and they have to be played by finding them through the quite cool mission select screen. 
Missions themselves are very linear, run down a corridor, gun down some guys, use your obligatory equipment, rescue hostages. Sometimes theres a bit of fun and you have to stealth your way into a location, but even the stealth mechanics are super barebones. Atleast the locales are quite unique, from drug labs hidden in rain forests, to metros of Japan.

Gunplay here is almost same as base Counter-Strike, though it will be much easier since the enemies are computer controlled and won't kill you in one hit, unless its a rocket launcher. Unlike CS, enemies don't drop their guns, so you have to use what the mission gives you. You can find some guns as you go along, with some being hidden in out of sight areas. Also you can have more than 1 primary weapon and theres a couple of new weapons. There is also new "equipment", like radio or a blowtorch, all of which can only be used when the mission tells you to, so any tactical uses or hidden stashes that could've spiced up the repetitve missions is moot.
Enemies are just terrorists with different weapons. Some will just sit behind cover while others will chase you relentlessly if you try to retreat, so be careful when hiding to reload. Snipers will usually be high on roof and easily noticeable due to the bright laser. Theres also new ones like machete and explosive vest dudes, who will charge you and whack you/explode. And worst of all: The rocket launcher bastards. They are like snipers but no laser, just 2 seconds before your entire existance gets wiped.
